title: About me
goal: Introduce yourself: say your name, where you are from, where you live and which languages you speak, and ask others the same.
intro:
In this unit you meet the Telugu pronouns and learn how to say 'I am...'. Telugu needs **no verb at all** to say who someone is (*నేను సారా*, I [am] Sara), but uses the verb *ఉండు* (uṇḍu) to say where someone is.

You'll also meet the core question words. Notice how Telugu asks 'where are you from?': *మీది ఏ ఊరు?* (mīdi ē ūru?), literally 'yours is which town?'

vocab.note: Oblique ఊరి-; in the town: ఊళ్ళో (ūḷḷō).
Before a noun: ఏ ఊరు? which town?
Present: ఉన్నాను, ఉన్నారు, ఉంది...; habitual: ఉంటాను.
నాకు తెలుగు వచ్చు, I know Telugu; negative: రాదు (rādu).

phrases.en: Where are you from? (lit. yours is which town?)
I'm from Vijayawada. (lit. ours is Vijayawada)

grammar.title: Pronouns and 'to be'
grammar.body:
**Who/what someone is**: Telugu uses no verb. *నేను సారా* (nēnu sārā) = I [am] Sara. With a noun describing *I* or *you*, the noun often takes a personal ending: *నేను విద్యార్థిని* (nēnu vidyārthini, I am a student). To deny, add **కాదు** (kādu): *నేను డాక్టర్ని కాదు* (I'm not a doctor).

**Where someone is**: use **ఉండు** (uṇḍu), whose present forms are:
నేను ఉన్నాను (unnānu) · నువ్వు ఉన్నావు (unnāvu) · అతను ఉన్నాడు (unnāḍu) · ఆమె / అది ఉంది (undi)
మేము / మనం ఉన్నాము (unnāmu, spoken unnām) · మీరు ఉన్నారు (unnāru) · వాళ్ళు ఉన్నారు (unnāru) · అవి ఉన్నాయి (unnāyi)

Note: **మేము** is 'we, but not you', **మనం** is 'we, including you'. The respectful ఆయన / ఆవిడ take the plural verb (*ఆయన ఉన్నారు*).

examples.en: We (you and I) are in Hyderabad.

grammar.title: Asking questions
grammar.body:
Question words go where the answer would go, usually just before the verb: *మీరు **ఎక్కడ** ఉన్నారు?* (Where are you?). The main ones: **ఏమిటి** what, **ఎవరు** who, **ఎక్కడ** where, **ఎలా** how, **ఏ** which.

For a **yes/no question**, add **-ā** to the last word: *ఉన్నారు* → *ఉన్నారా?* (are you there?), *వచ్చు* → *వచ్చా?* (do you know?).

dialogue.title: First day at the language class
dialogue.setting: Sara, an American student, meets Kiran in a Hyderabad college canteen.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.en: My name is Sara. And yours?

lines.speaker: Kiran
lines.native: నా పేరు కిరణ్. మీది ఏ దేశం?
lines.roman: nā pēru kiraṇ. mīdi ē dēsham?
lines.en: My name is Kiran. Which country are you from?

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.native: నేను అమెరికా నుంచి వచ్చాను. ఇప్పుడు హైదరాబాదులో ఉంటాను.
lines.roman: nēnu amerikā nunchi vachchānu. ippuḍu haidarābādulō uṇṭānu.
lines.en: I've come from America. Now I live in Hyderabad.

lines.speaker: Sara
lines.native: కొంచెం కొంచెం వచ్చు. నేను ఇక్కడ కొత్త.
lines.roman: konchem konchem vachchu. nēnu ikkaḍa kotta.
lines.en: A little bit. I'm new here.

lines.speaker: Kiran
lines.en: No problem. Which town are you from?

lines.speaker: Kiran
lines.en: I'm from Warangal. Nice to meet you.

culture: Telugu speakers identify strongly with their *ఊరు* (home town or village), so *మీది ఏ ఊరు?* is one of the first questions you'll be asked, even of a city-dweller born elsewhere. Telugu is the official language of two states, Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; the capital of Telangana, Hyderabad, has its own Urdu-flavoured Telugu, while coastal Andhra speech is considered the basis of the standard.
